objectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.
Explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to the pressure required to perfuse the systemic versus pulmonary circuits.
Describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow, and identify which valves separate which chambers or chamber-vessel pairs.

modules.description: Explore the external and internal structure of the heart, its four chambers, and the comparative thickness of the ventricular walls.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Locate and distinguish the right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle.
Identify the thick muscular myocardium of the left ventricle and explain its physiological significance.
instructions: Examine the 3D heart model from different angles.
Look at the differences between the atrium and ventricle walls.
Observe the thick muscular wall of the left ventricle.

components.scriptDescription: Calculates a sinusoidal scale oscillation on the target object to simulate a beating heart. Has configurable beating frequency (beats per minute) and pulse amplitude.

clips.changeMeaning: Shows the exterior structure of the human heart, introducing its muscular nature and position as a central pump.
clips.narration: Welcome to the Human Heart Anatomy lab. The heart is a specialized muscular pump responsible for maintaining constant circulation throughout the entire body. Before examining its internal path, notice its external shape, muscular layers, and orientation.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveals the inner chambers of the heart by disabling the exterior model and enabling the cross-section interior model along with localized labels.
clips.narration: By looking inside, we can identify the heart's four chambers. The upper receiving chambers are the right and left atria, which have relatively thin walls. The lower pumping chambers are the right and left ventricles, which feature highly muscular walls.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights and labels the thick myocardium wall of the left ventricle to compare it visually to the thinner right ventricular wall.
clips.narration: Take a close look at the muscular wall of the left ventricle compared to the right. The left ventricle's myocardium is substantially thicker. This is because the right ventricle only needs to pump blood a short distance to the lungs under low pressure, whereas the left ventricle must generate enough force to propel blood through the entire body.

modules.description: Examine the major vessels entering and leaving the heart, and the valves that prevent backflow.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the superior and inferior vena cava, pulmonary trunk/arteries, pulmonary veins, and the aorta.
Identify the four heart valves (tricuspid, pulmonary, bicuspid/mitral, aortic) and describe their role in directing flow.
instructions: Review the great vessels connected to the heart.
Examine the locations and functions of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves.

clips.changeMeaning: Points an interactive visual arrow at the Vena Cava and Aorta to illustrate the entry and exit points of systemic blood flow.
clips.narration: The heart is connected to several massive blood vessels. Deoxygenated blood returns from the body tissues through the superior and inferior vena cava into the right atrium. Once oxygenated, blood leaves the left ventricle through the aorta, the largest artery in the body, to supply systemic organs.

clips.changeMeaning: Repositions the arrow to highlight the pulmonary trunk/arteries and pulmonary veins, updating the dynamic text label accordingly.
clips.narration: Meanwhile, the pulmonary trunk exits the right ventricle and splits into the left and right pulmonary arteries to carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium through the four pulmonary veins.

clips.changeMeaning: Points the pointer arrow directly at the heart's valve structures, changing the text label to identify heart valves.
clips.narration: To prevent blood from flowing backward during contractions, the heart relies on four valves. The tricuspid and mitral valves—known as atrioventricular or AV valves—separate the atria from the ventricles. The pulmonary and aortic valves—known as semilunar valves—prevent blood from leaking back into the ventricles after it is pumped out.

modules.description: Follow a drop of blood as it journeys through the dual-loop circulatory system, exploring the pulmonary and systemic circuits.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace deoxygenated blood from the body to the lungs.
Trace oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the systemic circulation.
Explain how the synchronous action of the heart coordinates these two separate loops.
instructions: Follow the colored path lines representing blood flow.
Differentiate between the deoxygenated blue flow and the oxygenated red flow.

clips.changeMeaning: Enables a glowing blue flow line to visually trace the flow of deoxygenated blood from the body to the lungs.
clips.narration: Let's trace a drop of blood through the dual-loop circulation. Low-oxygen blood from the body enters the right atrium via the vena cava. It passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary valve and pulmonary arteries to the lungs, where it drops off carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen.

clips.changeMeaning: Disables the blue flow line and enables a glowing red flow line, tracing the systemic loop of oxygenated blood.
clips.narration: Now oxygenated, the blood returns via pulmonary veins to the left atrium. It flows through the mitral valve into the thick-walled left ventricle. From there, a powerful contraction drives the blood through the aortic valve and out through the aorta, distributing oxygen-rich blood to the entire body.

clips.changeMeaning: Enables both flow paths together to illustrate simultaneous, synchronous pumping action of both circuits.
clips.narration: In a healthy body, both loops run simultaneously. The two atria fill and contract together, followed immediately by the contraction of both ventricles. This synchronous coordination, secured by the continuous action of the valves, guarantees efficient, unidirectional blood flow throughout your entire life.
